title: Berabbi
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: We find a Tanna of a baraita called Berabbi, as in Makkot 5b: “Berabbi taught: If they did not kill, they are killed,” and Rashi explains that this was his name. In Chullin 11b Rashi explains: we do not know who he is, but [he was] one great in his generation. In Chullin 52b: “Berabbi taught: They did not say ‘mauled’,” etc., and Rashi explains: the name of a sage.

Apart from these three places, we find the title Berabbi with a personal name, such as Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, who is also called Rabban Gamliel Berabbi, as in Shabbat 115a and 151b and Kiddushin 32b, and Rashi explains: not that he was Rabbi’s son, but a great man is called Berabbi. Likewise Rabban Gamliel, the son of Rabbi, as in Jerusalem Talmud Challah 4:4, and Rabban Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehudah Nesia, as in Jerusalem Talmud Avodah Zarah 1:1. They also called Rabbi Yose ben Chalafta Berabbi, as in Sukkah 26a, and Rashi explains: Yose the sage, the sharpest in his generation; and in Pesachim 100a Rashi explains: every Berabbi is an expression for a great man — the reason of Rabbi Yose, who is a sage and the great man of the generation.

Hyman says that Rabbi Elazar HaKappar is always called Berabbi, as in Chullin 28a and 84b and Avodah Zarah 43a. In Berakhot 24b: “Rabbi Yochanan said: Achai Berabbi,” and Rashi explains: great in his generation, and wherever it says Berabbi this is its meaning. In Eruvin 53a Rabbi Yochanan called Rabbi Oshaya his teacher “Berabbi.”
In Kiddushin 80b Rabbi Yochanan called Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, when he heard this, “Berabbi.”

In Chullin 57a Rabbi Yose bar Chanina called Chizkiyah “Berabbi,” and Rashi explains that he was great in his generation. In Jerusalem Talmud Bikkurim 3:3 Rabbi Yannai called Yehudah son of Rabbi Chiyya, his son-in-law, “Yehudah Berabbi”; likewise in Shabbat, beginning of halakhah 2 of chapter 7, “Rabbi Sidor said: Yehudah Berabbi”; in Bava Batra, chapter 5, end of halakhah 4, “Rabbi La in the name of Rabbi Yehudah Berabbi”; Bereshit Rabbah 37:6 and 91:11, “Yehudah Berabbi”; and in Yoma 2:1, folio 8b, a dispute of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehudah Berabbi. Likewise in Rosh Hashanah 1:1, “Yehudah bei Rabbi said: A large account swallows a small account,” and Hyman proposes “Yehudah Berabbi.”

In Kiddushin 21b and Bekhorot 33b, “Yudan Berabbi used to expound,” and Rashi explains: Yudan was his name, and he was great in his generation; wherever they call him Berabbi it is an expression of wisdom and sharpness. In Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim 10:1 Rabbi Yose called Rabbi Simon “Berabbi.” After examination Hyman suggests that wherever the title Berabbi is mentioned with a personal name it should be written ברבי without a yod, and wherever it is [the person’s] name it should be בריבי with a yod. He reports examining all the places where it is mentioned with a personal name and finding them mostly without the yod, and in a few places with the yod, where Dikdukei Soferim reads without the yod. In the Responsa Noda BiYehudah, second edition, Orach Chayim, siman 113, it is cited that the Gaon Rabbi Yeshayah Pik asked him about this.

notes.text: The final סקי״ג is siman113, not13. The Hebrew ברבי/בריבי difference is explicitly retained even though the English label is shared; Hyman’s proposed distinction between an honorific and a personal name remains his own rule. ואך היה שמו is read as his name, ובברוכות as Berakhot; all full personal names and differing sources remain separate, without blanket son-of-Rabbi expansion.

The consulted Makkot 5b reads Beribbi’s statement about the witnesses, followed by his father’s question; Rashi there glosses that this was his name. This supports that occurrence, not a single identity for every occurrence or Hyman’s general distinction between ברבי as an honorific and בריבי as a personal name. His always and wherever formulations remain his own claims. The supplied Noda BiYehudah pointer is second edition, Orach Chayim 113; that exact printing and the claimed Dikdukei Soferim spellings have not been independently inspected here. The differing named bearers are not merged or all expanded as sons of Rabbi.
